stories.headline: Oil falls another 3% to a one-week low even as Washington names new Iran targets
stories.dek: Brent settled $88.58, down $3.59. US crude $82.36, down $2.65. Traders priced sanctions as less risky than missiles.
stories.caveman: Crude did not rally for the second day of Iran talk. Brent dropped 3.89 percent to $88.58 a barrel Tuesday. US West Texas Intermediate dropped 3.12 percent to $82.36. That is a one-week low. Monday it had already fallen more than $2. Traders decided economic pressure is not the same as rockets in Hormuz. Bessent's Monday kill-list still sat on the tape. Oil sold it anyway. A sanctions speech that cheapens barrels is a tell: the market thinks enough oil still sneaks out. Pump prices will lag. They do not fall as fast as a futures screen.
stories.why_it_matters: If barrels keep sliding while Treasury shouts asphyxiation, inflation fears ease and bond yields can drop. If Hormuz really shuts, this $88 floor vanishes in a day. Import islands pay either way.
stories.camps: Hawks wanted a shock. Traders priced a long mess, not a shutoff. Iran says any partner in the squeeze is at war. Drivers still pay last week's scare, not Tuesday's print.

terms.explain: The world oil sticker price, set in London. What most import countries pay.
The US oil sticker price. It usually sits a few dollars under Brent.
Cheapest in seven days. Monday already fell. Tuesday fell more.

stories.headline: S&P 500 edges up 0.3% as cheaper oil pulls the 10-year yield down to 4.63%
stories.dek: S&P 7,677.28. Dow 53,577. Nasdaq 26,151. Ten-year yield fell from 4.70%. Nvidia still reports after the US bell.
stories.caveman: Stocks liked cheaper oil more than they feared Iran. The S&P 500 rose 0.3 percent Tuesday to 7,677.28, a bit closer to its record from earlier this month. The Dow added 160 points. The Nasdaq climbed 0.7 percent. The 10-year Treasury yield dropped to 4.63 percent from 4.70 percent late Monday and 4.74 percent last Friday. High yields had been the summer headache. Oil's slide reined in the inflation scare that had pushed them up. Treasury's extra long-bond buybacks helped. Nvidia's report is still after the US close Wednesday — after this Taipei morning window. Nobody on this page pretends to know the number.
stories.why_it_matters: Yields down a few basis points cheapen mortgages and corporate debt. They also tell you the bond market is less scared of $4 gas than it was last week. Taiwan's dollar and foreign flows feel that shift before the next local open.
stories.camps: Bulls say oil down, stocks up, wait for Warsh. Bond bears say 4.63% is still far above the pre-war 3.97%. Families with floating loans feel the lag, not the tick.

terms.explain: The interest the US pays to borrow for ten years. When it jumps, mortgages and stocks all feel it.
One hundredth of a percent. A 7-point drop in the 10-year is a real move for bonds.
The US government buying its own old bonds to keep the long end from blowing out.

stories.image_alt: US stock and bond market trading floor or Wall Street scene

stories.headline: Gold tags a three-month high above $4,690, then fades before the Fed's inflation print
stories.dek: Spot hit $4,696.18, the most since May 14. It later slipped toward $4,622 as traders waited on PCE and Warsh.
stories.caveman: Bullion ran, then sat down. Spot gold tagged $4,696.18 an ounce Tuesday morning, the highest since May 14. By US midday it was off about 0.6 percent near $4,622. US futures also gave back the pop. The first burst was the Treasury's fatter long-bond buybacks, a softer dollar, and the Iran safe-haven bid. The fade was a round number and the wait for the Fed's favorite inflation gauge on Wednesday. Gold pays no interest. When yields fall it looks prettier. When traders want cash for a data day, it gets sold. Jewelers do not reprice every tick. Central banks still might.
stories.why_it_matters: A three-month high in gold is a fear meter, not a wage. If PCE comes in hot, yields can snap back and bullion gives the week back. If Warsh sounds lost, gold can run again.
stories.camps: Bulls say buybacks plus Iran equal a floor. Bears say $4,700 is a wall until the data. Mines like the print. People buying bangles this week pay the high, not the fade.

terms.explain: The cash price for a troy ounce now, not a futures contract for later.
The Fed's favorite inflation gauge. Out this week. Hot numbers can yank gold and bonds.
Money that runs to gold when wars and sanctions make other bets look shaky.

stories.headline: Jackson Hole opens Thursday; Warsh's first Fed keynote Friday is the rate tell
stories.dek: Symposium Aug 27–29. Theme: financial innovation and payments. Markets want more than his usual less-is-more silence.
stories.caveman: The mountain meeting is this week. Kansas City Fed hosts Jackson Hole Thursday through Saturday. New Chair Kevin Warsh gives his first big keynote Friday at 8 a.m. Eastern. Theme: financial innovation, payments, policy. He has spent the summer refusing to spoon-feed the next rate move, waiting on five task forces. Inflation is still above 2 percent. Trump still wants cuts. Bond traders still want a sentence they can price. TD and Deutsche Bank both told clients not to expect a full map, maybe a little less fog than July. No rate decision gets voted here. The speech still moves the dollar.
stories.why_it_matters: One hawkish paragraph can lift yields and knock Asian tech. One dovish shrug can do the opposite. Taiwan's Wednesday open will not have heard him yet. Friday will.
stories.camps: Hawks want him to say he can still hike. Doves want a path to cuts. Trump wants cheaper money. Shoppers want bread not a Wyoming podium.

terms.explain: The mountain gathering where Fed chairs often hint at the next year of rates.
New US central-bank boss. Friday is his first big Jackson Hole speech.
Telling markets the next rate move in advance. Warsh has tried not to.

stories.image_alt: Jackson Hole or Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh

stories.headline: Apple's first 2nm chip, the M6, lands in a new Mac mini; M5 Ultra claims 512GB of memory
stories.dek: 12-core CPU, 12-core GPU, dual 16-core Neural Engine. Preorder Tuesday. Ships Sept. 22. Memory inflation already in the price.
stories.caveman: Apple shipped a nanometer brag. The M6 is its first 2-nanometer chip, in a new Mac mini. Twelve CPU cores, twelve GPU cores, two 16-core Neural Engines. Apple says the fastest single thread it has sold, and about 30 percent more peak GPU compute for AI than M5. The M5 Ultra is the other headline: four dies glued as one, up to 36 CPU cores, 80 GPU cores, 512GB of unified memory at 1.2TB/s. Preorders opened Tuesday. Boxes arrive Sept. 22. The mini's sticker moved up as memory got scarce. On-device AI is the pitch. The wafers still come from Taiwan. Repair shops cannot swap that memory later.
stories.why_it_matters: If big models can live on a desk, cloud bills shift. If they cannot, this is another expensive box. Either way 2nm capacity gets locked, and gadget prices follow memory, not slogans.
stories.camps: Apple says run the model at home. Cloud vendors want the work in their halls. Chip bears say memory is the real tax. Buyers pay the tax at checkout.

terms.explain: A finer chip process. More transistors, more heat control, higher wafer prices.
Apple's on-chip block for local AI. M6 uses two 16-core engines at once.
One pool shared by CPU and GPU. You cannot add more after you buy.

stories.image_alt: Apple M6 and M5 Ultra chip announcement graphic

stories.headline: Stability AI raises $76 million from music majors and EA to keep selling generative tools
stories.dek: Series B brings the London image shop to $232 million raised. Universal, Sony, Warner, and Electronic Arts all in.
stories.caveman: The company behind Stable Diffusion is not dead. It raised $76 million Tuesday. Total haul: $232 million. The checks are not only funds. Universal Music, Sony Music, Warner Music, and game giant EA joined AMD Ventures and Pacific Alliance. CEO Prem Akkaraju, there since 2024, called it a vote for tools that help producers, not just prompt boxes. The plan is more creative-production software and a services arm. Stability spent a year signing studios to co-build, not just license output. A UK court mostly sided with it in one training-data fight. Getty's US case still walks. Musicians get a seat. Session players still wonder who owns the riff.
stories.why_it_matters: When labels buy the generator, the fight moves from court to contract. Training data remains the open wound. Artists without a major's lawyer get the old deal.
stories.camps: Stability says this is partnership. Rights hawks say the majors are buying the machine that chewed their catalogs. Staff get runway. Freelancers get a new competitor that never sleeps.

terms.explain: An image generator that kicked the open-model boom. The company behind it just raised again.
A middle-stage money round. Not the first, not the IPO.
Lawsuits over whether the model was fed copyrighted pictures without a license.

stories.image_alt: Stability AI or generative image-model branding

stories.headline: X sends cease-and-desist letters to Nitter, the login-free window onto its posts
stories.dek: Letters dated Aug. 24 gave until 5 p.m. Eastern Aug. 25 to kill instances and the repo. Nitter.net went dark pending counsel.
stories.caveman: The spare door is being welded. Nitter let people read X posts without an account, ads, or the app. X Corp. sent cease-and-desist letters Aug. 24. It accuses the project of scraping, skirting the API, and touching session tokens. The letter cites Texas computer-access law and the Lanham Act. Deadline: 5 p.m. Eastern Tuesday. Nitter.net went offline while its maker, known as Zedeus, called a lawyer. Other volunteer instances got the same paper. X had already tried to knock Nitter down with technical blocks. This time it brought a letterhead. Public posts become a product you must log in to see.
stories.why_it_matters: If the last no-login window dies, researchers, journalists, and people who will not make an account lose a way to read the town square. X keeps the gate.
stories.camps: X says theft of its API. Nitter's users say the posts were public. Lawyers will argue tokens and scraping. Moderators of small instances now hold a letter, not a server.

terms.explain: An open-source front end that showed X posts without logging in. The main site went dark Tuesday.
A lawyer letter that says stop or we sue. Not a court order. Still enough to kill a volunteer project.
The official pipe apps are supposed to pay for. Scraping grabs pages without that pipe.

stories.image_alt: X logo, the platform sending legal letters to Nitter

stories.headline: Gamma buys Accel-backed design startup Lica to build its own AI design lab
stories.dek: Founders Priyaa Kalyanaraman and Purvanshi Mehta will run the lab. Gamma last raised at a $2.1 billion value.
stories.caveman: Slideware is eating slideware. Gamma, the AI presentation shop, bought Lica on Tuesday. Lica started by turning screenshots into decks and videos, raised $4 million from Accel and friends, then made brand-safe clips for shops. Its founders will run a new research lab inside Gamma, aiming at custom voices for different audiences. Price undisclosed. Gamma is already worth $2.1 billion on paper. OpenAI bought a rival, NextSlide, earlier this month. The deck tools are consolidating before most offices have picked one. Designers who used to layout type now compete with a lab that wants to speak every brand.
stories.why_it_matters: When presentation apps merge, the remaining independents get squeezed. Offices may get prettier slides. The people who used to make them get fewer desks.
stories.camps: Gamma says multimodal is next. Lica's founders say they wanted a bigger lab. Design contractors see another tool that does their Tuesday. Accel sits on both sides of the trade.

terms.explain: A startup that builds slides from prompts. It just bought a design shop.
A small design-and-video startup. Its founders will run Gamma's new lab.
Text, pictures, and motion in one output. The new fight in office software.

stories.image_alt: Gamma and Lica teams or product after the acquisition

stories.headline: Pakistan says Munir's Tehran talks made 'significant progress' toward reviving the June deal
stories.dek: Interior minister Naqvi: meeting with President Pezeshkian ended on a positive note. Hormuz reopening and an expedited end were on the table.
stories.caveman: Islamabad came home talking progress. After Field Marshal Asim Munir's Monday in Tehran, Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi said Tuesday the sit-down with President Masoud Pezeshkian made significant progress. Pakistan's military listed three aims: no new escalation, reopen Hormuz, end the war faster. Iran's message, per Pakistani briefings, still starts with Washington moving first on the June Islamabad memo. Trump had called Munir last week to ask Pakistan to drag Iran back to the table. No new ceasefire text was published. 'Significant progress' is a phrase. Ships still count the strait.
stories.why_it_matters: If Pakistan can restart the June memo, oil and insurance calm down. If it is only a phrase, Tuesday's oil dip is the market shrugging, not a peace.
stories.camps: Islamabad wants a mediator's win. Tehran wants the US to go first. Washington wants Iran back at the table without giving the blockade. Tanker crews want a lane, not a communique.

terms.explain: The June pause deal Pakistan helped write. It asked Iran to reopen Hormuz and the US to ease the blockade.
Pakistan's top general. He spent Monday in Tehran trying to restart talks.
The skinny water door for a lot of the world's oil. Still not fully open.

stories.image_alt: Pakistani and Iranian officials after talks in Tehran

stories.headline: US asks the UN to stretch Sudan's Darfur arms embargo across the whole country — and over drones
stories.dek: Envoy Massad Boulos. France, Britain, Denmark back it. Russia, China, and Sudan's envoy do not. No vote Monday.
stories.caveman: The US wants the old Darfur weapons ban to cover all of Sudan, and to name drones in the text. Trump's Africa envoy Massad Boulos told the Security Council the war is being fed by more than 12 countries. UN political chief Rosemary DiCarlo said fancy weapons still mean outside help. Humanitarian chief Tom Fletcher said drones have hit markets, schools, fuel, and water; 1,100 civilians died in drone strikes from January to June. Sudan's envoy wants only a technical rollover of the Darfur ban, due to expire Sept. 12. Russia and China say a wider ban would hobble the army. No vote. The embargo as written still stops at Darfur's line.
stories.why_it_matters: Drones are the cheap way to hit a market. If the Council cannot name them, the war keeps buying parts. If it names them and Russia vetoes, the paper still expires in September.
stories.camps: Washington says choke the pipeline. Khartoum says do not tie the army's hands. Moscow and Beijing resist. People under the drones need a ceasefire, not a jurisdiction map.

terms.explain: A UN ban on sending weapons into a place. Darfur has one. The rest of Sudan does not.
Trump's senior Africa adviser. He asked the Council to widen the ban.
The paramilitary fighting Sudan's army. Both sides now fly drones.

stories.image_alt: Sudan conflict or UN Security Council debate on an arms embargo

stories.headline: Israeli strike wrecks a Gaza nutrition warehouse; at least seven Palestinians killed
stories.dek: MAP: food for children, pregnant women, breastfeeding mothers. Health chief: 12 of 34 oxygen stations still work. 1,288 killed since the October 'ceasefire'.
stories.caveman: The ceasefire is a word. Overnight into Tuesday an Israeli strike destroyed a warehouse of nutrition supplies for children and mothers, medical charity MAP said. Local medics counted at least seven Palestinians killed in strikes across Gaza. Health ministry chief Munir al-Bursh told Al Jazeera only 12 of about 34 oxygen stations still run. Gaza's health tallies: 1,288 Palestinians killed since the October 2025 ceasefire, 73,422 since October 2023. Trump told Fox on Aug. 17 that Israel should not be striking. The strikes continued. A warehouse of therapeutic food is not a rocket site. Hunger does not pause for a podium.
stories.why_it_matters: Killing the food store is how a paper ceasefire still starves. Oxygen going dark is a quieter death than a bomb, and just as final.
stories.camps: Israel cites security and kites. Hamas says the 15-point plan is already broken. Washington wants quiet without leverage. Parents in Gaza need formula, not another working group.

terms.explain: A medical charity. It said a warehouse of nutrition supplies was destroyed.
The US-brokered pause. Gaza officials say it lives in statements, not in streets.
Machines that keep hospital oxygen flowing. Most are already down.

stories.image_alt: Damage in Gaza after strikes that hit an aid warehouse

stories.headline: Iran and Oman sketch a temporary Hormuz corridor and a joint mine-clear — Tehran says the strait is still shut
stories.dek: Foreign ministers Araghchi and Albusaidi in Tehran Tuesday. Technical talks to follow on a permanent lane. US blockade and oil sanctions still the Iranian price.
stories.caveman: Two neighbors drew a maybe-lane. Oman's foreign minister sat with Iran's Abbas Araghchi in Tehran Tuesday. Joint statement: a phased framework, a temporary shared navigation corridor, a joint project to clear mines. More talks on a permanent corridor, traffic, and who runs the water. Iran's deputy foreign minister said later this is not a reopening. The strait stays closed until Washington lifts the naval blockade, oil sanctions, and frozen assets. Trump has claimed US control and US minesweeping. Iran says those claims are pressure. Coordinates were not published. Insurers will not send a ship on a sentence.
stories.why_it_matters: A paper corridor can calm oil. A corridor without coordinates and without US-Iran movement is a press release. Fertilizer and grain still sit behind the same choke.
stories.camps: Muscat wants a lane it can police with Iran. Tehran wants US concessions first. Washington wants credit without giving the blockade. Crews want charts, not frameworks.

terms.explain: A maybe-lane through Hormuz, sketched by Iran and Oman. Not a full reopening.
Taking explosives out of the water. The June deal had put that on Iran. This version says joint.
Iran's foreign minister and Oman's. They signed the Tuesday statement.

stories.image_alt: Iranian and Omani foreign ministers meeting in Tehran on Hormuz

stories.headline: Liane Moriarty returns to Monterey: Big Little Truths is out, 10 years after Big Little Lies
stories.dek: Crown. $34. The Pierces, Mackenzie, and friends tangle in another school-gate crime. On-sale Tuesday.
stories.caveman: The Monterey moms are back. Liane Moriarty's Big Little Truths landed Tuesday, a decade after Big Little Lies made the school run a crime scene. Same circle, ten years on, another ugly secret tied to their children's school. Crown put a fat hardcover price on it: $34. It is not a prestige-small novel. It is the rare beach book that still makes bookstores build a pile. HBO already taught the world the first plot. This one has to survive people who think they know these women. School-gate gossip is still unpaid labor. Moriarty just invoices it.
stories.why_it_matters: A franchise this big sets the fall table for commercial fiction. It also keeps selling a story about women managing other people's violence with casseroles.
stories.camps: Fans want the old trio. Critics will ask if a sequel can bite. Booksellers want the stack. The parents in actual school WhatsApp groups already live the unpaid version.

terms.explain: Moriarty's 2014 novel, later an HBO series. The new book picks up ten years later.
The Tuesday a hardcover is allowed to sell. Tuesday was that day.
Novels built to sell in piles. Not a slur. A business.

stories.image_alt: Cover of Liane Moriarty's Big Little Truths

stories.headline: Edwidge Danticat's Dèy, a Miami-to-Haiti novel of a mall shooting and withheld grief, is out today
stories.dek: Knopf. $29. 256 pages. Title is Kreyòl for mourning. Magnolia, a Haitian American realtor, tells no one she survived.
stories.caveman: Danticat's first novel in nearly a decade arrived Tuesday. Dèy. Knopf. Two hundred fifty-six pages. Magnolia sells houses in Miami. She is in a mall for her daughter's birthday when a gunman fires. She hides. She lives. She tells nobody. The book is cut into shelter-in-place verbs: Run, Hide, F(l)ight, then Dèy. Haiti is not background. Her parents went home and now live under gangs and stolen houses. PW called it delicate and wonderful. The title is the Kreyòl word for mourning. Joy still sits at the grandmother's table. Trauma that stays unspoken does not stay small.
stories.why_it_matters: A novel that treats a US mall shooting and Haitian gang rule as one nervous system is not a tour. It is how a lot of families actually split their fear.
stories.camps: Knopf is betting on a quiet 256-page book, not a doorstop. Haitian readers will weigh the Kreyòl. US crime headlines rarely follow the realtor home to Brooklyn and Port-au-Prince.

terms.explain: Haitian Kreyòl for mourning. The novel's title and last section.
The narrator. She survives a mall shooting and keeps it from her family.
Danticat won a National Book Critics Circle award for that story collection.

stories.image_alt: Cover of Edwidge Danticat's novel Dèy

stories.headline: John Manuel Arias's Crocodilopolis, a Costa Rican dynasty novel, hits shelves with a 150,000-copy bet
stories.dek: Bloomsbury. $29.99. PW called it lush and suspenseful. Two rival brothers, one political family, one old country.
stories.caveman: Another Tuesday pile. Crocodilopolis by John Manuel Arias, Bloomsbury, almost $30, 150,000-copy first printing per PW's August calendar. Two brothers from a Costa Rican political clan go at each other. PW's review said lush and suspenseful. It is not a New York kitchen. It is a Central American house with a long memory and a crocodile in the title. Big printings on literary sagas are a bet that readers still want family as nation. Bookstores will put it beside the Moriarty stack and hope some of that traffic walks left.
stories.why_it_matters: A 150,000-copy literary printing means a publisher spent real money on a non-US dynasty story. If it stalls, the next Latin American novel gets a smaller truck.
stories.camps: Bloomsbury wants a saga that travels. Reviewers want the sentences. Costa Rican readers will judge the clan. US buyers may only see the crocodile.

terms.explain: A novel about rival brothers in a Costa Rican political family. Out Tuesday.
How many copies the publisher made before seeing a sale. A show of confidence, or of hope.
Fiction where the house is the country. Marriages and grudges do state work.

stories.image_alt: Cover of Crocodilopolis by John Manuel Arias

stories.headline: Ingram opens Covered to booksellers and librarians, a new pipe for digital review copies
stories.dek: About 200 beta publishers already on it. Catalogs and ordering promised this fall. Aimed at Edelweiss and NetGalley.
stories.caveman: The warehouse just built a reading room. Ingram, the giant that ships most US bookstore orders, opened Covered on Monday to every bookseller, librarian, and trade reader. Digital review copies first. Some 200 publishers from the beta are already posting galleys. You read in the browser or a new app, EPUB or PDF. No print galleys in the plan. Audio later. Catalogs and ordering due fall. Banners in 2027. Ingram wants a slice of the Edelweiss and NetGalley desk. Indie stores already drown in PDFs. A new login does not give them more staff hours. It does decide which titles get a human eye before pub day.
stories.why_it_matters: Whoever owns the galley pipe owns attention. If Covered works, small presses without Edelweiss budgets might reach stores. If it is just another tab, the same 200 publishers keep the window.
stories.camps: Ingram says one desk for catalogs, galleys, orders. Edelweiss and NetGalley will not clap. Indie buyers want fewer logins, not more. Authors on IngramSpark get a paid DRC button.

terms.explain: Ingram's new site for digital catalogs and review copies. Opened to stores and libraries this week.
A free early ebook for people who might stock or review the book.
The two pipes stores and reviewers already use. Covered wants that desk.

stories.image_alt: Publishers Weekly report on Ingram's Covered platform launch

stories.headline: UN: Myanmar rights hit a new low as Rohingya abuses and illegal rare-earth mines boom
stories.dek: 3.6 million displaced. 12.4 million hungry. 302 new Kachin mine sites since 2021. Rare-earth trade peaked near $1.4 billion.
stories.caveman: Geneva put it bluntly Tuesday. Myanmar's human-rights office report, covering mid-2025 to mid-2026, says conditions are the worst yet. The army and the Arakan Army both stand accused of killing, torture, forced labor, and blocking Rohingya returns. Displacement: 3.6 million. Acute hunger: 12.4 million. About 400,000 mothers and children are acutely malnourished. The money story is dirt: satellite counts show 302 new rare-earth sites in Kachin since 2021, Shan sites up from 12 to 85 after the coup. Trade peaked around $1.4 billion in 2023, mostly to China. Toxic runoff is in local water and in rivers heading to Thailand — arsenic, lead, mercury, manganese. Phones need those metals. Villages drink the waste.
stories.why_it_matters: A conflict economy that sells rare earths to the energy transition is not a side note. It is how the war pays for itself, and how the water dies.
stories.camps: The UN names both the junta and the Arakan Army. Neither answered Reuters. China buys the rock. Phone makers are downstream. Rohingya families are under it.

terms.explain: An ethnic armed group that now holds much of Rakhine. The UN says it also abuses Rohingya.
Metals for magnets, EVs, phones. In Kachin they are dug in a lawless boom.
A Muslim minority, already driven out in earlier purges, still hunted in this report.

stories.image_alt: UN or Reuters image from Myanmar's conflict and mining crisis

stories.headline: Guterres: two confirmed famines at once is a 'shameful milestone' — Sudan and Gaza
stories.dek: WFP's Carl Skau: Sudan staple foods up almost 40% since February. Gaza famine reversed after October, recovery still fragile.
stories.caveman: The UN chief used a hard word Tuesday: shameful. Last year was the first time this century two famines were confirmed at once, in Sudan and in Gaza. Guterres told the Security Council not to wait for the next official stamp. WFP's Carl Skau said an oil tanker stuck in Hormuz can mean one less meal in Sudan. Sudan's basic food costs are up almost 40 percent since February. He saw Gaza in famine last July, then again in January after the October pause: better, not safe. Action Against Hunger counted more than 900 attacks on Sudanese food systems since 2023. Being a woman there, their CEO said, statistically predicts starvation. Resolution 2417 already exists. The Council is being asked to use it.
stories.why_it_matters: Famine is a policy result, not weather. Two at once means the warning system is working and the politics are not.
stories.camps: UN agencies want action before the next declaration. Big powers will bargain the wording. Mothers in Sudan and Gaza need food convoys, not milestones.

terms.explain: Guterres's phrase for two confirmed famines at once, in Sudan and Gaza.
A 2018 Council text that says starving civilians is a method of war. Rarely enforced.
Acting head of the World Food Programme. He briefed the Council on Tuesday.

stories.image_alt: UN briefing on famines in Sudan and Gaza

stories.headline: UN chiefs warn a Hormuz-Red Sea-Black Sea 'triple chokepoint' is pushing millions toward hunger
stories.dek: Hormuz moves a third of world fertilizer. Istanbul Strait grain down 40% year on year. Sudan, Yemen, Gaza, Lebanon most exposed.
stories.caveman: Three doors are jammed at once. Guterres and WFP's Skau told the Council Tuesday that Hormuz, the Red Sea, and the Black Sea are a triple chokepoint. Hormuz carries about a third of global fertilizer. Restrictions there cut supply while oil is still 36 percent above pre-war. Grain through the Istanbul Strait is down 40 percent from a year ago. Conflict hunger has tripled in eight years even as aid budgets shrink. Sudan, Yemen, Gaza, and Lebanon sit in the blast radius of other people's shipping fights. A war in one strait becomes a smaller sack of flour in another capital. Truckers and bakers feel it before diplomats do.
stories.why_it_matters: Food inflation is not only drought. When fertilizer and grain lanes clog, harvests next year shrink. Importing countries cannot vote the ships through.
stories.camps: UN agencies want the lanes opened and farms protected. Belligerents treat chokepoints as leverage. Importers pay. Families skip a meal.

terms.explain: A skinny sea lane that a lot of food or fuel must pass. Close it and prices jump everywhere.
Plant food. A third of it moves through Hormuz. No fertilizer, smaller harvests later.
The passage for Black Sea grain. Shipments down 40 percent year on year, WFP said.

stories.image_alt: Shipping or food-aid image tied to the UN chokepoint warning

stories.headline: WFP is turning away six of seven malnourished Afghan children for lack of money
stories.dek: Skau's aside in the same Council briefing. Gaza showed a fragile recovery is possible. Afghanistan shows a funding cliff.
stories.caveman: One line in Tuesday's food briefing should not have been an aside. WFP's Carl Skau said the agency is turning away six in seven malnourished children in Afghanistan because the money is gone. Not because the war next door took the trucks. Because donors did not pay. Gaza, he said, had a glimmer after the October pause and more aid. Afghanistan is the opposite glimmer: the clinics are there, the ration is not. A child refused at the door does not appear in a famine declaration. They just go home thinner. Funding gaps do the work bombs do, slower.
stories.why_it_matters: A 6-out-of-7 refusal rate is a policy choice by capitals that still fund other wars. Malnutrition at that scale becomes stunting, then a generation.
stories.camps: WFP wants checks. Donor capitals are tired and elsewhere. Afghan families already lived through a government collapse. The seventh child is not a statistic to the six who were sent away.

terms.explain: The UN's food agency. It is turning most malnourished Afghan children away this month.
A child too thin right now. It can kill fast. It can also reverse with food — if the food is there.
The hole between what agencies asked for and what states paid. That hole is the door.
